rows.quick: Quick answerNumb toes cycling often starts with pressure you only notice during a ride. First check whether your shoe has enough room and the fastening is not tight. Avoid changing your entire position immediately: compare one small adjustment at a time and ask a clinician about recurring or lasting numbness.
rows.article: The problem: numb toes cycling Your shoes feel comfortable at home. On the road, a burning sensation develops beneath the forefoot. Your toes tingle or feel less distinct. Loosening the shoe may help briefly, but the problem returns later. Notice exactly where you feel it. Is the pressure on top, along the outer edge or beneath the ball? Does it start in both feet together? Differences between your feet may matter more than the size printed on the box. Record when it happens too. Is it linked to warmth, long climbs or harder pedalling? Are you wearing different socks from those used when fitting the shoes? A shoe that feels pleasant when walking need not provide the same support while cycling. You need not wait until your whole foot becomes numb. Stop loading it when tingling develops and check the pressure. Bike position cannot explain every foot symptom. Include symptoms away from the bike in your notes. Background: space, pressure and foot support Your foot sits between an insole, an upper and a fairly stiff outer sole. The fastening keeps it in place. Excessive tension can create local pressure. Tightening further therefore cannot automatically correct an unsuitable shoe shape. Length and width are different measurements. A longer shoe may still be too narrow at the forefoot. Conversely, an oversized shoe may let your foot slide. You might then tighten the fastening harder to compensate for that movement. Cleats connect the foot to the pedal. Their position changes where support is felt beneath the shoe. Moving them backwards can be a trial for forefoot pressure, but does not prove they caused it. Rotation and available movement also matter. An insole occupies space. A thicker replacement can therefore create a new pressure spot. Compare changes to the insole, sock and fastening separately. Avoid buying more support immediately when the shoe already feels cramped. Bike position affects the whole arrangement. Reaching for the pedals may change how you load the foot. However, a burning forefoot does not reliably prove that the saddle is too high. Checking the shoe first avoids unrelated adjustments elsewhere. An online photograph cannot assess sensation, circulation or nerve function. The pattern of symptoms remains important. The NHS guidance on pins and needles advises medical assessment for recurring or persistent symptoms. Use a calculator for dimensions, not diagnosis. How to approach it with bike fitting Record your starting point. Photograph both cleats directly from below. Mark their outlines with removable tape. Note your shoes, socks, insoles and when the problem starts. Record the pressure location for each foot. This makes a later comparison more useful than relying on memory alone. Check shoe space first. Use the socks you normally ride in. Check that the toes have room without the heel lifting freely. Look for pressure along the forefoot edge. A visible mark is a clue, not a diagnosis. Ask a shop or fitter to compare shoe shapes when uncertain. Reduce unnecessary fastening pressure. Loosen slightly without letting the foot slide. Check for a folded tongue or sock. Choose a short, easy ride close to home. Stop if numbness returns. Do not continue simply to complete a planned testing duration. Comfort should not depend on ignoring reduced sensation. Only then consider the cleat. For local forefoot pressure, discuss a small backward trial, for example 2–3 mm. This is a cautious fitting trial, not medical treatment. Stay within the slots and follow the specified tightening torque. Do not change rotation simultaneously. Ask a clinician about symptoms at rest, night pain, swelling or radiating tingling. Continuing to guess after 3–4 careful adjustments is unhelpful. h1: Cycling climb time: plan your effort
rows.quick: Quick answerEstimating your cycling climb time starts with distance, average gradient, body mass and a usable FTP estimate. The calculator combines these with fixed assumptions about your bike and resistance; wind, stops and steep sections can change your actual time. Treat the result as preparation and check your effort during easy practice rides.
rows.article: The problem: estimating cycling climb time You are planning a hilly ride and want to know when you will reach the top. The distance looks manageable, but the elevation profile leaves you unsure. Perhaps you still have further to ride afterwards. A fast first climb is not automatically a good start. On previous rides, you may have started too hard. A steeper section forced you to push a heavy gear or stand. Your expected arrival time kept slipping. A calculation can then create pressure instead of clarity. Comparing yourself with a riding partner does not always help. Your mass, bikes, positions and available power differ. An average gradient also cannot describe every change along the climb. A steady road differs from alternating steep and flat sections. This guide helps you interpret an estimate and check it practically. You do not need a record attempt. The aim is a workable starting point, allowing for traffic, conditions and personal experience. Background: what the calculation includes The climb calculator uses distance and average gradient. You also enter body mass, bike type and FTP. Here, FTP provides a power reference, not proof that you can sustain it everywhere. The calculation selects a power factor using a distance category. That is a simplification. A short, steep climb can take longer than a longer, shallow climb. The distance category therefore measures neither your capacity nor the actual duration directly. Do not treat the suggested power as an instruction. The physics model adds resistance from climbing, rolling and air. It also accounts for drivetrain losses. Body mass and a default bike mass together form the total mass. The chosen bike type also supplies fixed assumptions about aerodynamic resistance and surface. There is no personal measurement of your position. Wind is not entered separately. A headwind can change your actual speed without the calculator knowing. Luggage, road conditions and stops may also differ from the assumptions. Calculated time comes from distance divided by estimated speed. This assumes a steady situation. It does not predict braking, corners or transitions between sitting and standing. A reliable time is unavailable outside the calculation range. A suitable position helps you control the bike and assess your effort. It does not guarantee a time saving. Online tools let you compare inputs, but cannot establish your personal limit for sustained exercise. Keep the calculation alongside your ride notes, rather than giving it priority over them. How to approach it: from estimate to practice ride Check the route profile: Record the climb length and the source of its average gradient. Look for the steeper sections too. Keep distance in kilometres and gradient in percent to avoid mixing units. Plan a safe route back and allow for breaks. An arrival time must never decide whether you continue in unsafe conditions. Record your inputs: Use current body mass and a recent FTP estimate with a known origin. Record how that value was obtained. Choose the closest bike type and remember that its mass is a default value. Use the climb calculator to record your starting point. Consider carried luggage when assessing uncertainty in the result. Compare assumptions: First change only FTP to another value supported by your own records. Check the effect on time and power. Then consider changing gradient if your route information supports a different value. Do not select a favourable number to obtain a desired finish time. This comparison shows sensitivity to assumptions, not an individual training prescription. Check your reach while climbing: Record which hand position you use on the climb. On a quiet, safe section, check whether you can shift and brake from that position. You need to look ahead without letting go of the controls. If a brake lever is difficult to reach, check whether your model offers reach adjustment. Have it adjusted according to manufacturer instructions if needed, then check braking operation. Record the original setting; keep handlebar components within their clamping marks and respect specified torque values. Ride two to three easy trials: Use a familiar climb and change only one element at a time. Keep route and conditions as comparable as possible. Afterwards, record position, selected gear, perceived effort and any discomfort. Only then compare actual time with the estimate. Restore your previous setup if control or comfort worsens. Do not make the next ride harder simply to achieve the calculated power. Allow flexibility and recognise warnings: Avoid connections that depend on achieving the predicted time. Stop for pain or unsafe handling. Ask a fitter to review a persistent position problem. Pain at rest or at night, swelling and radiating tingling need medical assessment. If pain remains after three to four careful adjustments, seek help instead of continuing to experiment. Further reading What is cycling FTP? helps you assess which power value to enter and understand the uncertainty attached to it. Cycling power and speed: what changes? explains why the same effort can produce different speeds along your route. Mountain bike fit: control and movement helps you check position and control when your climb includes unpaved sections. Endurance bike fit: comfort over distance helps you consider the distance still remaining after the summit. The climb calculator makes assumptions visible so you can compare different route inputs deliberately. Frequently asked questions Does the displayed time include my breaks? No, the model calculates time from distance and estimated riding speed. Add room for stops yourself when planning. Allow for junctions and waiting too. A precise number on the screen does not mean your arrival is predictable to the nearest minute. Why does average gradient not match every section? An average summarises the whole climb. It can hide steep ramps and flatter sections. Look at the route profile alongside the input field. Your gearing needs to suit the sections you actually ride, rather than just the average shown in the calculator. Should I maintain the suggested power throughout? No. The power factor is a model choice based on distance. It is not an individual exercise test. Use experience and conditions to ride more gently whenever needed. Choosing a lower effort does not mean you have failed to follow the calculation correctly. Does a different saddle height predict a time saving? No, the calculator does not measure saddle height or predict its effects. Adjust only for a clear position or control question. Record the starting position and test carefully. sections.title: The problem: estimating cycling climb time
sections.text: You are planning a hilly ride and want to know when you will reach the top. The distance looks manageable, but the elevation profile leaves you unsure. Perhaps you still have further to ride afterwards. A fast first climb is not automatically a good start. On previous rides, you may have started too hard. A steeper section forced you to push a heavy gear or stand. Your expected arrival time kept slipping. A calculation can then create pressure instead of clarity. Comparing yourself with a riding partner does not always help. Your mass, bikes, positions and available power differ. An average gradient also cannot describe every change along the climb. A steady road differs from alternating steep and flat sections. This guide helps you interpret an estimate and check it practically. You do not need a record attempt. The aim is a workable starting point, allowing for traffic, conditions and personal experience.

sections.title: Background: what the calculation includes
sections.text: The climb calculator uses distance and average gradient. You also enter body mass, bike type and FTP. Here, FTP provides a power reference, not proof that you can sustain it everywhere. The calculation selects a power factor using a distance category. That is a simplification. A short, steep climb can take longer than a longer, shallow climb. The distance category therefore measures neither your capacity nor the actual duration directly. Do not treat the suggested power as an instruction. The physics model adds resistance from climbing, rolling and air. It also accounts for drivetrain losses. Body mass and a default bike mass together form the total mass. The chosen bike type also supplies fixed assumptions about aerodynamic resistance and surface. There is no personal measurement of your position. Wind is not entered separately. A headwind can change your actual speed without the calculator knowing. Luggage, road conditions and stops may also differ from the assumptions. Calculated time comes from distance divided by estimated speed. This assumes a steady situation. It does not predict braking, corners or transitions between sitting and standing. A reliable time is unavailable outside the calculation range. h1: Endurance bike fit: comfort over distance
rows.quick: Quick answerEndurance bike fit means finding a position that stays usable later in the ride. Discomfort may become noticeable when you hold the same position longer or become tired; start by checking support and reach. Record your measurements, compare one small change on easy rides, and extend the distance only while the position remains comfortable.
rows.article: The problem: endurance bike fit The first kilometres feel good, but later you lean more heavily on your hands. You shift around the saddle or look for another grip. Perhaps each hand position still feels usable on its own. Yet continuing to ride comfortably becomes increasingly difficult as the ride goes on. A short shop trial does not always reveal that. A comfortable commute cannot tell you everything about a longer outing either. You use the same bike for longer, perhaps with different clothing or luggage. Write down what differs before changing the bike position itself. Record where discomfort begins and which position you are using then. Does it appear on a long flat stretch or after climbing? Does your posture feel uncomfortable, or do the brakes also become difficult to reach? That distinction helps you choose a focused check. A long ride is not a test you must finish despite pain. Stop when symptoms or reduced control call for it. Background: a usable position leaves room to move A position for long rides depends on the relationship between support and reach. Your seating needs to remain usable while your hands use different positions. The brakes must be accessible from the position in which you ride. Looking only at bar height therefore gives an incomplete picture. Higher bars may feel different, but they cannot guarantee comfort for everyone. Reach to the hoods and your place on the saddle still count. Change both together and you cannot tell which adjustment made a difference. Measure contact points before you move any components. The bike's category does not decide whether its position suits you either. An endurance bike can be awkwardly built for your body. Conversely, your current bike may become usable within its permitted settings. Compare the actual position and component options, rather than relying only on the label. Several circumstances often change on a longer outing. You might wear different shorts, carry luggage or ride harder with a group. Changing your position at the same time makes comparison difficult. Keep these factors as consistent as possible during your first test rides. An online calculation helps organise your starting measurements. It cannot show how you sit or steer later in a ride. Your own notes provide additional information about that experience. A fitter can then assess how contact points and movement work together, without inferring the cause of symptoms from a single measurement. How to approach it with bike fitting Describe your usual long ride. Record route, effort, luggage, clothing and hand positions. Note when the position becomes less comfortable. Describe what still worked well before that point too. Use earlier experiences; you do not need another long ride with symptoms to complete this overview. Save your current measurements. Place the bike upright on level ground. Use a tape measure and spirit level for saddle height, distance to the hood and bar height difference. Name reference points and take a side photograph. The bike fit calculator helps set body measurements alongside these bike measurements as a starting point. Check support and controls. Do you stay in the same place when changing hand positions? Can you brake without first sliding forwards? Ask a fitter to observe if your seating keeps changing. Avoid simply moving the saddle forwards to solve a difficult reach to the bars. Choose one small, reversible change. When bar height needs attention, discuss a permitted increase. A 2–5 mm step is a cautious test example, not a universal measurement or treatment. Have a mechanic check whether your system allows it. Follow manufacturer limits, cable clearance requirements and torque settings, and check the controls before departure. Start with familiar rides. Compare two to three easy rides wearing the same clothing and using similar effort. Use only safe hand positions with reliable access to the brakes. Record comfort, saddle movement and reach at the beginning and end. Extend ride duration gradually afterwards, only while the position remains comfortable. Assess the whole ride and stop in time. More comfortable hands do not count as success if seating or control access gets worse. Stop for new symptoms or reduced control and restore the recorded safe starting position. Have uncertain installation checked before riding again. For pain persisting after three to four careful adjustments, seek assessment from a fitter and a clinician where appropriate. Stop experimenting for pain at rest, night pain, swelling or radiating tingling. Seek earlier medical assessment rather than waiting for your planned long outing. New loss of sensation also needs assessment. Adding kilometres is not a way to get used to those warning signs. Cycling climb time: plan your effort helps you include expected climbing duration in preparation for your outing. The bike fit calculator offers a starting point for comparison with your own contact points. Frequently asked questions Should I immediately sit higher for a long ride? Not automatically. Start with the position you currently use and record what becomes uncomfortable later. Higher bars change one part of the whole position. Check reach, seating and control access before deciding which adjustment you want to compare on your own bike during a series of easy rides. Can I try a new position just before an event? Allow enough easy comparison rides before relying on the new position. A long outing with a group makes calm assessment harder. If that preparation is missing, seek advice first. Always keep your previous measurements so that returning to the recorded safe position remains mechanically possible if needed. Will different cycling shorts help assess my bike position? Different shorts change the conditions of your comparison. Initially wear the same well-fitting clothing during a position trial. If you later compare clothing, leave bike measurements unchanged. Record your experience without immediately treating a more comfortable feeling as proof that the position itself is right for you. How do I know whether an improvement lasts later? h1: What is cycling FTP?
rows.quick: Quick answerThe question ‘what is cycling FTP’ concerns a reference for sustained cycling effort, expressed in watts. Our calculator either accepts a known value or estimates FTP from a test using a fixed factor. Always record the test method and conditions; the result does not describe guaranteed power for every ride or position.
rows.article: The problem: what is cycling FTP in your situation? Your cycling computer asks for FTP, but you do not know what to enter. Perhaps you received an estimate after a ride. A training programme displays another number. It can seem as though one of them must be wrong. Uncertainty can remain after a test too. You ride indoors in a different position from outdoors. You might use a different power meter. You remember the final number, but no longer remember exactly how you performed the test. That makes comparison difficult. A higher number can feel encouraging, although the conditions have changed too. A lower number likewise cannot explain the difference without additional information. The number alone is not a complete record of your effort. What you need is a traceable starting point. This guide explains what our calculator does and what you should record yourself. You can then use a value without immediately drawing conclusions about health, talent or your ideal riding position. Background: test factors are calculation conventions FTP is a power reference used when planning and comparing effort. This calculator lets you enter a known FTP. That value remains unchanged. The calculator does not verify the quality of the original estimate by accepting it. For the twenty-minute method, the model uses 95 percent of the entered test power. For the ramp method, it uses 75 percent. These are factors from our calculation rules. They are not universal descriptions of how every body responds to a test. A calculation example makes the distinction clear. Entering 200 watts for the twenty-minute test produces 190 watts. That comes from multiplying by 0.95. It does not prove that you personally can sustain exactly 190 watts for a prolonged effort. The input must also match the selected method. An arbitrary peak power is not a useful substitute for the output of a ramp protocol. Follow your test provider's instructions. This guide does not prescribe a maximal exercise test itself. Yet both frames carry the same size label. You wonder whether you need familiarisation or whether the bike does not fit. Perhaps you are comparing two bikes you already own. Your shoulders relax on one, while you keep sliding on the other. Contact points could explain the difference. However, another saddle, handlebar or pair of shoes can also affect the comparison. A short test ride cannot answer every question. You might ride without luggage, with different pedals or on unfamiliar ground. That means you are comparing more than riding position. Write down the particular difference you want to investigate first. Use a comfortable existing position as your starting point. If your current position hurts, use it only as a measurement reference. The aim is a useful comparison, rather than an exact copy of an existing problem. Background: frame dimensions are not contact points A frame size does not describe where your hands ultimately rest. Stem length, handlebar shape and brake hoods also matter. The saddle has its own shape too. Two saddle noses at identical distances can therefore still feel different. Stack and reach help you compare frames. They describe the vertical and horizontal distance from the bottom bracket to the top of the head tube. They describe the frame, rather than your complete position. Check the manufacturer's geometry diagram to confirm the reference point used. On an assembled bike, also measure your actual support points. Choose a recognisable saddle reference and record it. Measure to the hand position you normally use. That might be the brake hood on a road bike or the grip on a mountain bike. Saddle height alone does not provide a complete comparison. Record setback, pedal position and crank length too. Different shoes or pedals can change the connection between your foot and the bike. Keep these consistent during testing where possible. Intended use also determines which similarities matter. A mountain bike needs room for movement on trails. A triathlon bike adds armrests as support points. Identical handlebar heights do not automatically mean equivalent positions on such different bikes. A table or calculator can reveal differences, but cannot assess handling or pain. Body measurements also cannot tell you how much adjustment a particular component permits. Always check manufacturer information alongside your measurements. If your desired position falls outside the adjustment range, ask a fitter whether another size makes more sense. Choose a familiar, quiet route where you can brake and turn safely. Avoid comparing a relaxed commute with a hard training session. Wear the same shoes and use similar clothing and luggage. Ask which components the shop allows you to adjust during a test ride. Measure your baseline: Stand the bike upright on level ground and use a tape measure and spirit level. Record saddle height, setback, and the height and distance of your hand position. Use the bottom bracket as your common reference. Record the measurement points and take a side photograph. h1: Mountain bike fit: control and movement
rows.quick: Quick answerMountain bike fit starts with safe braking and enough room to move above the bike. Check your seated position while pedalling gently, but also assess what happens when you stand and descend. Record saddle height and bar position, change one thing at a time, and begin on an easy, familiar trail before attempting harder terrain.
rows.article: The problem: assessing mountain bike fit You feel comfortable on the cycle path, but keep sliding forwards on climbs. During a descent, the saddle feels obstructive. You grip the bars harder and search for the brake levers. These are different experiences, which do not automatically share the same cause. Perhaps you transferred your measurements from a road bike. Perhaps this is your first mountain bike with suspension. The bike moves beneath you and the ground demands constant attention. A familiar seated height cannot explain the whole experience. Even experienced riders notice differences after changing bars, shoes or their usual route. Record where discomfort appears: seated climbing, standing or braking downhill. Include whether you are tired and whether the trail matches your abilities. A useful first check concerns control access and room to move. You do not need a difficult descent to assess an adjustment. Begin somewhere you can stop calmly and try again. Background: your position changes with the terrain On a mountain bike, you alternate between sitting and standing. When seated, the saddle, pedals and hands support your body. Standing removes saddle support. You then need to move without losing access to the brakes. Assess saddle height and clearance above the saddle separately. A comfortable pedalling height can become obstructive on a descent. A dropper post can offer different positions if your bike supports one. However, it cannot make incorrect installation safe. Bar shape, width and brake levers determine where your hands work. Examine your actual grip, rather than a bar measurement alone. You need to brake from that grip. Holding the bars tightly throughout a descent will not fix a difficult lever reach. Suspension and tyres also affect how the bike feels on trails. Changing them can disrupt your comparison of riding positions. Use the relevant manufacturer settings as your starting point and record them. This guide does not prescribe universal pressures or suspension settings. Technique and route choice remain important too. A position that looks convincing in a photograph might prove awkward while braking. Conversely, uncertainty on a difficult trail does not automatically mean your frame is wrong. First choose surroundings where you feel in control. Online body measurements help establish a starting position. They cannot show how you move over roots or brake on a slope. A fitter can assess your position if uncertainty persists. A mechanic can help with controls and installation; instruction may help with trail skills. How to approach it with bike fitting Keep the test terrain simple: Choose a familiar trail with clear visibility and space to stop. Begin without technical obstacles. Check brakes, tyres and secure components before comparing your riding position. Record your usual route, shoes and pedals. Note whether the problem appears while seated or standing. Do not ride a harder section solely to prove that an adjustment works. Measure your seated baseline: Use a tape measure from the bottom bracket to a fixed saddle reference. Also record setback, bar height and hand position. Take a photograph showing your reference points clearly. If the bike has a dropper post, measure its normal pedalling position and label that clearly. Check permitted insertion depth and installation instructions. Distinguish operating the post from changing its fixed installation height. Check hands and movement: Test brake access while stationary with secure support, then at low speed. Stand briefly on the pedals in a clear area. Check whether you can move without unexpectedly contacting the saddle. Have the levers adjusted according to their instructions if you cannot reach them properly. Avoid cutting bars as your first experiment. An irreversible modification does not belong in a simple comparison. Choose one small adjustment: If investigating whether your saddle is slightly high, try lowering it by 2–5 mm, for example. Use this only as a cautious trial within its adjustment range. It is not a fixed mountain bike correction or pain treatment. Keep tyre pressure and suspension unchanged during this comparison. Follow tightening torque requirements and saddle rail and seatpost limits. Ask a mechanic for help if you lack the tools or installation knowledge. Test and recognise your limit: Take two to three easy rides per change while the bike remains comfortable and safe. Compare seated pedalling, gently standing and braking on the same route. Stop if control worsens and restore the recorded safe position. Stop and seek medical assessment for pain at rest or at night, swelling or radiating tingling. Consult a fitter or doctor if symptoms persist after three to four careful adjustments. Do not keep riding through symptoms just to complete a technical section. rows.description: Why does the same power produce a different speed? Understand wind, gradient and resistance, compare your inputs and check your position on easy rides.

h1: Cycling power and speed: what changes?
rows.quick: Quick answerThere is no fixed conversion between watts and kilometres per hour when comparing cycling power and speed. Gradient, mass and resistance change the result; our calculator uses a simplified model without separate wind input. Check conditions and your records before attributing a lower speed to your fitness or bike setup.
rows.article: The problem: comparing cycling power and speed You are producing the same power as last week but travelling more slowly. Your cycling computer shows familiar wattages. Yet every kilometre seems to take longer. You might wonder whether something is wrong with your bike setup. The opposite happens too. On another road, a higher speed comes easily. That feels like progress, but you do not know how much the conditions contribute. Comparing only the averages of both rides gives no clear answer. A ride also includes corners, junctions and times when you coast. Average power and average speed summarise those different situations. They do not describe one steady stretch of road. A calculator cannot supply the missing history of that ride. You therefore need to understand which comparisons are meaningful. This guide helps you separate resistance, position and inputs. It can prevent repeated harder efforts or adjustments made simply to achieve a theoretical speed. Start with conditions that you can actually record. Background: three contributions to required power Our model adds power for climbing, rolling and aerodynamic resistance. It then accounts for drivetrain losses. It uses body mass and bike mass together. You also select gradient, surface and bike type for the corresponding assumptions in the calculation. Climbing includes the effect of gravity. Greater total mass requires more power at the same gradient and speed in this model. For rolling, the calculation uses a fixed resistance value per surface. This does not measure your particular tyres, pressure or road texture. For aerodynamic resistance, the model uses a fixed value per bike type. It does not measure body shape or position. In the formula, aerodynamic power grows with the cube of speed. This applies within the assumptions, including a situation without separately modelled wind. You therefore cannot conclude that twice the power always produces twice the speed. The contributions change with speed and gradient. Headwinds and tailwinds change the real situation but are absent as separate inputs. Riding beside others or receiving shelter is not personally calculated either. The calculator can estimate required power from speed. In reverse, it searches for a speed matching the entered power. That search has limits. A calculation-range warning does not prove that the displayed boundary will become your actual speed. Meanwhile, gearing determines the relationship between cadence and speed. A bigger gear does not supply extra power by itself. Our gearing formula links wheel circumference and tooth ratio to distance travelled per pedal revolution. Keep that mechanical relationship separate from the resistance you must overcome. How to approach it: compare the same situation first Choose a clear stretch of road: Find a familiar section where steady riding is safe. Avoid a comparison based on a whole ride containing many stops. Record wind direction, surface, gradient and whether you rode alone. Keep your speed safe and watch traffic. The aim is to understand your measurements, not to stare continually at a screen while riding. Check your inputs: Record body mass and bike mass with their units. Choose a bike type and surface that approximate your situation. Do not select a gradient because it produces a nicer result; use available route data and acknowledge uncertainty. The power and speed calculator helps you record the combination. Remember that fixed resistance values do not replace personal measurements. Change one assumption: Keep every other field unchanged and alter only gradient, for example. Examine the effect on power or speed. Then compare another surface if it reflects the roads you actually use. This shows which part of your question the model can answer. You cannot reliably imitate wind by arbitrarily selecting a different bike type. Compare a usable position: Take a side photograph and record where your hands hold the bars. Check that you can look ahead and reach the brakes safely from that position. Also note whether you can maintain it gently without repeatedly searching for support. Explore your usual hand positions before moving components. Choose a position with reliable support and control for the comparison. If that requires a different handlebar setup, keep your original measurements and have a mechanic check manufacturer limits, cable length and torque specifications. Compare two to three easy rides: Test only one setup change at a time and keep your route familiar. Record comfort and control alongside power and speed. Note changed wind even when that makes the comparison less tidy. Restore your recorded starting position if things worsen. Avoid drawing aerodynamic conclusions from one fast ride; the model has not measured your position. Stop chasing the result: A theoretical speed is not a safe minimum. Stop for pain or loss of control. Ask a fitter to assess a recurring position problem instead of repeatedly adjusting further. Pain at rest or at night, swelling or radiating tingling need medical assessment. Seek help too if pain remains after three to four careful adjustments. A calculator cannot explain those warning signs. Further reading What is cycling FTP? helps you understand the power reference you are using before comparing a predicted speed. Cycling climb time: plan your effort shows how gradient and estimated power combine to affect your expected uphill time. Triathlon bike fit: support in aero discusses support when you consider a different position and want to assess it safely. Road bike fit: your three contact points helps you examine control and comfort in your current position systematically. The power and speed calculator compares individual assumptions without making its output a promised road speed. Frequently asked questions Can I enter a headwind in the calculator? No, this calculator has no separate wind input. Record wind with your ride notes and treat differences from the calculation as uncertainty. Do not simply choose a heavier surface to replace a headwind. That changes a different assumption without actually modelling the wind. Will a bigger gear make me faster? At the same cadence, a bigger gear changes calculated speed. That does not mean you can sustain that combination. Required effort still depends on resistance and gradient. Use gearing to pedal appropriately, rather than treating it as proof that extra power is available. Why does my ride average differ from the result? The calculation describes a steady situation. Your ride probably contains changing speeds, braking and sections without pedalling. That ride average is not the same input as one constant section. Compare conditions carefully before attributing any difference between the numbers to your bicycle. Does a faster ride prove my position is better? No, wind and route may also have changed. First assess whether you steer and brake safely and remain comfortable. Keep your previous measurements and repeat gently. An individual assessment of aerodynamic resistance requires more than a speed figure from this calculator alone.Compare power and speed using traceable inputs and check the result against your own ride notes.Compare power and speed

sections.title: The problem: comparing cycling power and speed
sections.text: You are producing the same power as last week but travelling more slowly. Your cycling computer shows familiar wattages. Yet every kilometre seems to take longer. You might wonder whether something is wrong with your bike setup. The opposite happens too. On another road, a higher speed comes easily. That feels like progress, but you do not know how much the conditions contribute. Comparing only the averages of both rides gives no clear answer. A ride also includes corners, junctions and times when you coast. Average power and average speed summarise those different situations. They do not describe one steady stretch of road. A calculator cannot supply the missing history of that ride. You therefore need to understand which comparisons are meaningful. This guide helps you separate resistance, position and inputs. It can prevent repeated harder efforts or adjustments made simply to achieve a theoretical speed. Start with conditions that you can actually record.

sections.title: Background: three contributions to required power
sections.text: Our model adds power for climbing, rolling and aerodynamic resistance. It then accounts for drivetrain losses. It uses body mass and bike mass together. You also select gradient, surface and bike type for the corresponding assumptions in the calculation. Climbing includes the effect of gravity. Greater total mass requires more power at the same gradient and speed in this model. For rolling, the calculation uses a fixed resistance value per surface. This does not measure your particular tyres, pressure or road texture. For aerodynamic resistance, the model uses a fixed value per bike type. It does not measure body shape or position. In the formula, aerodynamic power grows with the cube of speed. This applies within the assumptions, including a situation without separately modelled wind. You therefore cannot conclude that twice the power always produces twice the speed. The contributions change with speed and gradient. Headwinds and tailwinds change the real situation but are absent as separate inputs. Riding beside others or receiving shelter is not personally calculated either. The calculator can estimate required power from speed. In reverse, it searches for a speed matching the entered power. That search has limits. A calculation-range warning does not prove that the displayed boundary will become your actual speed. Meanwhile, gearing determines the relationship between cadence and speed. A bigger gear does not supply extra power by itself. Our gearing formula links wheel circumference and tooth ratio to distance travelled per pedal revolution. Keep that mechanical relationship separate from the resistance you must overcome.

Choose a bike type and surface that approximate your situation. Do not select a gradient because it produces a nicer result; use available route data and acknowledge uncertainty. Change one assumption: Keep every other field unchanged and alter only gradient, for example. Examine the effect on power or speed. Then compare another surface if it reflects the roads you actually use. This shows which part of your question the model can answer. You cannot reliably imitate wind by arbitrarily selecting a different bike type. Compare a usable position: Take a side photograph and record where your hands hold the bars. Check that you can look ahead and reach the brakes safely from that position. Also note whether you can maintain it gently without repeatedly searching for support. h1: Road bike fit: your three contact points
rows.quick: Quick answerYour road bike fit starts with the relationship between saddle, pedals and brake hoods: one uncomfortable contact point does not identify the wrong measurement. First record your current position and describe where support or control feels lacking. Then check your seating, foot contact and hand reach before trying one small, reversible adjustment.
rows.article: The problem: checking your road bike fit Your road bike feels comfortable at first, but you keep changing position during the ride. You slide towards the saddle nose or increasingly use the tops of the bars. Perhaps you avoid the drops because reaching the brakes feels difficult there. Sometimes the uncertainty starts with a new saddle, different shoes or a borrowed bike. The frame size seems right, yet the whole position feels different. You want to identify what needs attention without moving everything at once. Record where discomfort starts and what you are doing then. Are you riding easily, into the wind or downhill? Are your hands on the hoods or in the drops? Note whether the same symptom occurs away from cycling too. This guide helps you check all three contact points together. The aim is a usable starting position for your rides. Low handlebars in a photograph do not prove that you can ride safely and comfortably. Background: three contact points form one position The saddle supports your seating, pedals connect your feet to the bike and handlebars provide hand contact. Distances between them determine where your body has room. Moving one point changes its relationship to the others too. Moving a saddle forwards, for example, shortens the distance to the brake hoods. It also changes your seating relative to the pedals. Do not automatically use that movement to solve distant handlebars. First check whether you can find a usable seating area on the saddle itself. At the front, more than stem length matters. Bar height, bar shape and brake hood placement together determine your hand position. The height difference between saddle and bars is called drop. Equal drop on two bikes does not automatically produce the same position. Your shoes belong in this comparison too. Different shoes, pedals or cleats change the contact beneath your feet. Record those changes before attributing a difference entirely to the saddle. A tight shoe closure also needs a different check from an unreachable brake lever. Your ride determines which position needs to remain usable. Riding steadily, braking and looking behind involve different demands from sitting for a photograph. Fatigue, clothing and your chosen effort can also change the experience. Compare rides that are reasonably similar. An online calculation organises body measurements and provides a starting point. It cannot see a loose component or check whether you can reach your brakes. It cannot explain pain or replace an assessment of your movement on the bike either. How to approach it with bike fitting Create a useful baseline: Stand your bike upright on a level floor and take a side photograph. Gather a tape measure, spirit level and notebook. Record saddle height from the bottom bracket centre to an identifiable point on the saddle. Record saddle position, bar height and distance to the hoods too. Describe your measuring points, shoes and pedals. You can then actually return to the same position later. Check the controls first: While stationary, check whether both brake levers are within comfortable hand reach. Then try gentle braking and steering somewhere safe. Use only hand positions that let you reach the necessary controls safely. Ask a mechanic to check hood position or lever reach if uncertain. Do not rotate bars or hoods arbitrarily to hide a problem. Check that cables remain clear when steering too. Assess seating and foot contact: Describe whether you slide forwards, sit unevenly or seem to reach for the pedal. Check shoe closure and cleat attachment. Then choose one specific question for your trial. If you have reason to investigate excessive saddle height, lowering it by 2–5 mm is one small trial example. This is not a prescription for pain. Keep the old measurement and do not change saddle tilt simultaneously. Investigate hand reach next: Does your seating remain usable while the hoods feel distant? Record whether distance or height feels difficult. Discuss a suitable stem or permitted height increase with a mechanic. Respect manufacturer insertion markings, clamping zones and torque settings. Do not force extra height beyond the permitted assembly. The bike fit calculator helps compare your body measurements with your starting position. Compare calmly and reverse when necessary: Test one change over two to three easy rides while you remain symptom-free. Keep route, clothing and effort comparable. Record seating, hand pressure and control access after each ride. Stop for new pain, lost sensation or reduced control. Restore the recorded safe position; have uncertain installation checked before riding again. A trial is only useful when you know what changed. Recognise the limit of self-adjustment: Stop experimenting for pain at rest, night pain, swelling or radiating tingling. Seek medical assessment then. If pain persists after three to four careful adjustments, consult a fitter and, where appropriate, a clinician. No, height alone cannot tell you whether a position is usable. A change also needs to suit your rides and movement. Assess whether you can keep looking, steering and braking as needed. rows.description: Unsure about your bike setup measurements? Learn to record saddle height, reach and bar drop with clear reference points, then test one small change.

h1: Bike setup measurements: record your position
rows.quick: Quick answerYour bike setup measurements need reference points you can find again using the same method. Record saddle height, setback, tilt and hand position with clearly described measuring points, alongside the fitted components. Then check which measurement relates to your question; a difference on paper alone is no reason to change a comfortable position.
rows.article: The problem: confusing bike setup measurements You want to restore your saddle after maintenance, but your old note contains only a number. You cannot remember where the tape started. Perhaps you measured along the seat tube, while now measuring directly to the saddle nose. The difference looks like a fitting problem, but could come from your method. The same thing happens when comparing two bikes. Saddle to bar distance looks equal, yet your hands sit further away. Or a new saddle has the same height but supports you in a different place. A list of numbers alone cannot explain that. This guide helps you build a complete, repeatable record. You learn which measurements answer different questions and which components to record alongside them. You can then track a change, reverse it or discuss it with a fitter. A measurement sheet does not prove that every number suits your body. Background: reference points give numbers meaning Saddle height describes the distance between the bottom bracket centre and a chosen point on the saddle surface. Record which point you use and how you hold the tape. A different saddle shape can change that point. Compare the measuring method and component as well as the result. Saddle setback is a horizontal distance relative to the bottom bracket. You might choose the saddle nose as an identifiable reference and record that choice. A shorter saddle nose changes this measurement without necessarily making the same change to your seating location. Saddle tilt describes something else: the angle of your chosen measuring surface. For the handlebars, height and distance are separate questions. Drop describes the vertical difference between saddle and bars. Reach to the hood describes where your hand rests. A distance to the bar centre does not fully record hand position because bar shape and hoods also matter. Frame reach and stack belong to frame geometry. They do not directly describe the distance from your saddle to your hands. The stem, spacers and bar add their own dimensions. Keep frame specifications separate from your measured contact points. Crank length runs from the bottom bracket centre to the pedal axle centre. Record shoes, pedals and cleats too. These details identify which components were present during measurement. A component change can be a reason to measure and compare again. A calculator can offer direction, but cannot check your reference points. A small difference between measurements may be measuring variation. First establish whether the difference is repeatable before moving components. How to approach it with bike fitting Create a consistent measuring setup: Stand the bike upright on a level surface. schemas.description: Gevoelloze tenen tijdens het fietsen? Controleer schoenruimte, sluiting en schoenplaatjes. Ontdek een rustige testvolgorde en wanneer je hulp vraagt.

mainEntity.name: Moet ik fietsschoenen een maat groter kopen?

acceptedAnswer.text: Niet automatisch. Vergelijk eerst lengte, voorvoetbreedte en ruimte bovenop de voet. Een grotere maat kan extra schuiven geven terwijl de drukrand blijft. Neem je fietssokken mee bij het passen. Laat verschillende schoenvormen vergelijken in plaats van alleen de maat te verhogen.

mainEntity.name: Kan ik zonder schoenplaatjes testen?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dat kan een andere belasting geven, maar verandert meerdere dingen tegelijk. Zie het niet als sluitend bewijs over de oorzaak. Zorg dat schoenen en pedalen samen veilig werken. Laat een losse schoenplaatjesbevestiging nooit zitten als geïmproviseerde manier om extra beweging toe te staan.

mainEntity.name: Waarom helpt losser draaien maar tijdelijk?

acceptedAnswer.text: De sluitdruk kan een onderdeel zijn, terwijl de schoenvorm of binnenzool ook meespeelt. Tijdelijke verlichting vertelt niet welke oorzaak doorslaggevend is. Noteer waar de druk terugkomt. Blijft de voet tintelen na het stoppen, vraag dan medische beoordeling in plaats van steeds losser te rijden.

mainEntity.name: Moet links hetzelfde staan als rechts?

acceptedAnswer.text: Niet iedere voet heeft dezelfde vorm. Kopieer daarom geen millimeters zonder de plaatsing te controleren. Leg beide uitgangspunten afzonderlijk vast. Grote verschillen of eenzijdige aanhoudende klachten vragen een gerichte beoordeling, niet zomaar een extra correctie met ringen of een andere zadelstand.

Een al omgerekende waarde opnieuw met een testfactor vermenigvuldigen geeft een andere uitkomst. Bewaar het originele verslag. Ontbreekt de methode, behandel het getal dan als onzeker in plaats van een precieze vergelijking te maken. Kies de passende invoer: Gebruik ‘bekend’ voor een bestaande FTP-waarde. Kies de twintigminutenmethode alleen voor het bijbehorende testresultaat. Gebruik de oplopende methode uitsluitend wanneer je weet welke vermogenswaarde jouw protocol daarvoor levert. De FTP-calculator helpt de rekenstap controleren. Een calculator kan ontbrekende informatie over een test niet achteraf reconstrueren. Beschrijf de meetomstandigheden: Noteer binnen of buiten, koeling, gebruikte fiets en vermogensmeter. Volg de handleiding voor controle en kalibratie van je apparaat. Gebruik bij vergelijkingen bij voorkeur dezelfde meetbron en dezelfde uitvoering. Leg ook vast of je een andere houding gebruikte. Vergelijk niet ongemerkt een comfortabele buitenrit met een test op een onbekende binnenopstelling. Houd je opstelling gelijk: Meet je zadelhoogte met een meetlint en maak een zijfoto. Noteer de meetpunten en handpositie voor latere vergelijkingen. Houd deze afstelling tijdens je vergelijking gelijk, zodat je niet tegelijk een andere houding onderzoekt. Plaats de fietstrainer volgens de handleiding op een stabiele ondergrond. Gebruik steeds dezelfde voorgeschreven voorwielondersteuning en oriëntatie van de fiets. Controleer na verplaatsen de bevestiging volgens de fabrikant en herstel je vastgelegde maten als onderdelen zijn verschoven. Controleer de herhaalbaarheid rustig: Rijd twee tot drie rustige ritten met dezelfde opstelling. Controleer of ondersteuning, handpositie en bereik van de bediening gelijk blijven. Dit zijn geen FTP-tests en je hoeft daarbij geen maximale inspanning te leveren. Los een verschoven of onveilige opstelling eerst op; test daar niet doorheen. Is een houdingswijziging nodig, leg die apart vast en stel de vermogensvergelijking uit. Plan een eventuele latere test volgens een passend protocol, met de omstandigheden opnieuw vastgelegd. Stel het getal niet boven klachten: Stop de inspanning bij pijn en ga niet door om een test af te maken. Bespreek terugkerende houdingsproblemen met een fitter. sections.text: Bepaal je vergelijking: Noteer waarvoor je beide fietsen wilt gebruiken en welke houding nu prettig voelt. Schrijf ook op wanneer ongemak ontstaat. Kies een rustige, bekende route waarop je veilig kunt remmen en keren. Vergelijk geen ontspannen woonrit met een zware training. Neem dezelfde schoenen en gebruik vergelijkbare kleding en bagage. Vraag bij een winkelproefrit welke onderdelen tijdelijk aangepast mogen worden. Meet de uitgangspositie: Zet de fiets recht op een vlakke ondergrond en gebruik een meetlint en waterpas. Leg zadelhoogte, setback en de hoogte en afstand van je handpositie vast. Gebruik de trapas als gemeenschappelijke referentie. Noteer je meetpunten en maak een zijfoto. Schrijf cranklengte, zadelmodel en pedaaltype erbij. Meet een opvallend verschil opnieuw voordat je er een aankoopbeslissing op baseert. Meet de tweede fiets hetzelfde: Gebruik dezelfde ondergrond, hulpmiddelen en referentiepunten. Vergelijk eerst de contactpunten en daarna de framegegevens. Zo zie je of het verschil uit het frame of de opgebouwde onderdelen komt. Een afwijkende stuurpenlengte is op zichzelf geen afkeurreden. Controleer wel of een passende positie met toegestane onderdelen haalbaar blijft. Laat twijfel over montage of stuurgedrag door een fietsenmaker beoordelen. Een moeilijk bereikbare hendel los je niet op door tijdens de hele afdaling krampachtig vast te houden. Vering en banden beïnvloeden eveneens hoe de fiets op terrein aanvoelt. Een verandering daarin kan je vergelijking van de zithouding verstoren. Gebruik de bijbehorende fabrikantinstellingen als uitgangspunt en noteer wat je gebruikt. Deze gids geeft geen universele druk of veringsafstelling. Techniek en routekeuze blijven daarnaast belangrijk. Een houding die op een foto overtuigt, kan tijdens het remmen onpraktisch blijken. Omgekeerd betekent onzekerheid op een moeilijk pad niet vanzelf dat je frame verkeerd is. Kies eerst een omgeving waarin je controle hebt. Online lichaamsmaten helpen een uitgangspositie vastleggen. Ze laten niet zien hoe je over wortels beweegt of op een helling remt. Bij blijvende twijfel kan een fitter je positie beoordelen. Voor bediening en montage helpt een fietsenmaker; voor terreinvaardigheden kan begeleiding nuttig zijn.

sections.title: Zo pak je het aan met bikefitting
sections.text: Maak het testterrein eenvoudig: Kies een bekend pad met goed overzicht en ruimte om te stoppen. Begin zonder technische hindernissen. Controleer remmen, banden en vastzittende onderdelen voordat je de zithouding vergelijkt. Noteer je gebruikelijke route, schoenen en pedalen. Schrijf op of het probleem zittend of staand ontstaat. Rijd geen moeilijker stuk uitsluitend om te bewijzen dat een verandering werkt. Meet je zittende basis: Meet met een meetlint van de trapas naar een vast punt op het zadel. Noteer ook setback, stuurhoogte en handpositie. Maak een foto waarop je meetpunten herkenbaar zijn. Heeft je fiets een verstelbare zadelpen, meet dan de normale trapstand en noteer die duidelijk. Controleer de toegestane insteekdiepte en montagevoorschriften. Verwar de bediening van de pen niet met het veranderen van de vaste montagehoogte. Controleer handen en beweging: Test het rembereik eerst stilstaand met veilige ondersteuning en daarna bij lage snelheid. Sta kort op de pedalen op een overzichtelijk stuk. Controleer of je kunt bewegen zonder onverwacht tegen het zadel te komen. Laat remhendels volgens hun handleiding aanpassen als je ze niet goed bereikt. Zaag een stuur niet als eerste proef korter. Een onomkeerbare ingreep hoort niet bij een eenvoudige vergelijking. Kies één kleine wijziging: Wil je onderzoeken of je zadel iets te hoog staat, probeer dan bijvoorbeeld 2–5 mm lager. Gebruik dit alleen als voorzichtige proef binnen het verstelbereik. Het is geen vaste mountainbikecorrectie of behandeling van pijn. Houd bandendruk en vering tijdens deze vergelijking gelijk. Volg aanhaalmomenten en grenzen voor zadelrails en zadelpen. Laat een fietsenmaker helpen wanneer je gereedschap of montagekennis mist. Test en herken je grens: Maak twee tot drie rustige ritten per wijziging, zolang de fiets prettig en veilig blijft. Vergelijk zittend trappen, rustig opstaan en remmen op dezelfde route. Stop bij slechtere controle en herstel de vastgelegde veilige stand. Bij pijn in rust of 's nachts, zwelling of uitstralende tintelingen stop je en vraag je medische beoordeling. Blijven klachten na drie tot vier zorgvuldige aanpassingen bestaan, raadpleeg dan een fitter of arts. Blijf niet door een klacht heen rijden om een technische passage alsnog te halen.

Lichaamsmaten geven hooguit een vertrekpunt. Ze bepalen niet zelfstandig je beste armsteunhoogte, heuphoek of wedstrijdhouding. Een fitter kan je tijdens het trappen bekijken en de combinatie beoordelen. De fabrikant bepaalt welke steunen, bevestigingen en verstelstanden technisch toegestaan zijn.

Houd schoenen, kleding en zadel gelijk. Kies buiten een overzichtelijke plek zonder druk verkeer. Gebruik binnen alleen een traineropstelling die geschikt is voor je fiets en stabiel staat.

Noteer ook de afstand tussen de steunen en de stand van de handgrepen. Maak foto's van de bevestigingen. Zo kun je terug naar je uitgangspositie zonder op je geheugen te vertrouwen.

Controleer bediening en steun: Neem de houding aan met veilige ondersteuning en controleer of je handen ontspannen blijven. Kijk vooruit zonder je blik langdurig op de voorband te richten. Oefen de overgang naar de remmen eerst stilstaand en daarna bij lage snelheid.

Pas één onderdeel aan: Wil je een iets hogere steun onderzoeken, probeer dan bijvoorbeeld 2–5 mm verhoging als het systeem dat toestaat. Gebruik uitsluitend goedgekeurde onderdelen en de voorgeschreven bevestiging. Deze kleine proefstap is geen voorgeschreven behandeling of universele triatlonmaat.
Niet ieder systeem biedt zulke stappen. Forceer geen tussenstand en gebruik geen geïmproviseerde vulstukken. Volg aanhaalmomenten, zadelrailgrenzen en de instructies voor het betreffende ligstuur.

Test zonder je houding te forceren: Vergelijk één wijziging tijdens twee tot drie rustige ritten, zolang je comfortabel en veilig blijft. Noteer zicht, steun, trappen en hoe gemakkelijk je bij de remmen komt. Stop bij verslechtering en herstel je vastgelegde veilige positie.

De houding ziet er laag uit, maar voelt onderweg niet vanzelfsprekend. Dat kan gebeuren op een echte triatlonfiets en op een racefiets met een ligstuur. Misschien heb je de positie van een andere fietser overgenomen. Misschien zijn de armsteunen veranderd zonder de rest opnieuw te controleren. Wat op een foto overtuigt, hoeft bij jouw lichaam en fiets niet bruikbaar te zijn. Noteer wanneer je uit de houding komt. Gebeurt het meteen, bij harder trappen of pas later in een lange rit?
